title: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
summary: How ViT turns an image into patch tokens, where its 86M parameters live, and how to adapt a pretrained checkpoint: new head, resized position embeddings, schedules, augmentation, LoRA and LP-FT.
outcomes: Compute a ViT's sequence length and parameter counts from image size, patch size and model width
Explain why position embeddings must be interpolated to fine-tune at a higher resolution, and why bicubic is used
Set up a fine-tuning recipe with warmup, cosine decay, augmentation and layer-wise learning-rate decay
Choose between linear probing, LoRA, full fine-tuning and LP-FT for a given data and deployment setting

lessons.title: Turning an image into a sequence of patch tokens

blocks.md:
Say you have 4,000 labeled food photos in 101 classes and want a classifier. Training a Vision Transformer (ViT) from scratch on that is a bad bet. Dosovitskiy et al. (2020) note that ViT has much less image-specific inductive bias than a CNN: locality and 2D neighborhood structure are not built into its layers, so it has to learn them from data.

Their own numbers show the effect. The same ViT-B/16, fine-tuned and evaluated on ImageNet, scores 77.91% top-1 when pre-trained on ImageNet-1k (1.3M images), 83.97% when pre-trained on ImageNet-21k, and 84.15% on JFT-300M. Pretraining data size moves accuracy by 6 points.

So the practical recipe is **transfer learning**: start from a checkpoint someone pre-trained on a large dataset, replace its classification layer, and continue training (**fine-tune**) on your small labeled set. Before we can fine-tune well, we need to know exactly what is inside the checkpoint, starting with how an image becomes something a transformer can read.

Recall from the prerequisite: a transformer encoder maps a sequence of vectors to a sequence of vectors of the same size, using attention to mix information between positions. ViT's only new idea is how to make that sequence from pixels.

scenes.caption: Toy: a 64x64 RGB image cut into 16x16 patches gives a 4x4 grid, so 16 patches. Each patch holds 16 x 16 x 3 = 768 pixel values. Colors mark the four grid rows.
Flatten the grid in raster order (row by row) and project each 768-number patch to a D-dimensional vector with one shared matrix E. The 2D layout is now gone: the transformer sees a list.
Prepend one learnable [class] vector (CLS). It belongs to no patch; its job is to collect information from all patches through attention. The sequence is now 16 + 1 = 17 tokens.
Add a learnable position embedding to each slot (e0 for CLS, e1 to e16 for patches). Without it, attention could not tell r0c0 from r3c3, because attention treats its inputs as an unordered set.

blocks.caption: Eq. 1 of the ViT paper. Image H x W with C channels, patch size P. E has shape (P^2 C) x D and E_pos has shape (N+1) x D.

blocks.prompt: A standard ViT-B/16 checkpoint takes 224x224 RGB images with 16x16 patches. How many tokens does the encoder see, and how many numbers are in one flattened patch?
blocks.reveal:
224 / 16 = 14 patches per side, so $N = 14 \times 14 = 196$ patches, plus 1 CLS token: **197 tokens**.

One patch is $16 \times 16 \times 3 = 768$ numbers. For ViT-Base the model width is also $D = 768$, so E happens to be a square 768 x 768 matrix. That is a coincidence of this configuration, not a rule: ViT-L/16 also has 768-number patches but $D = 1024$.

blocks.md:
Three design choices from the paper matter later when we fine-tune:

- **CLS token.** Like BERT's [class] token, a learnable vector is prepended. Its state at the output of the last layer, after a final LayerNorm, is the image representation $\mathbf{y}$. The classification head reads only this vector.
- **Learnable 1D position embeddings.** One learned D-vector per slot (197 of them at 224). The authors report no significant gain from 2D-aware variants.
- **Head.** An MLP with one hidden layer during pre-training, a single linear layer at fine-tuning time.

blocks.title: The ViT forward pass, end to end

scenes.caption: Input side: a 224x224 image becomes 196 flattened patches, each projected by the same matrix E, then CLS is prepended and position embeddings are added. Result: 197 vectors of size D.

The encoder is the pre-norm transformer from the prerequisite course: LayerNorm then multi-head attention, LayerNorm then a 2-layer MLP with GELU (a smooth ReLU), each with a residual add. Every patch can attend to every other patch from layer 1.
Only the CLS position is read out. Its final state goes through LayerNorm and then the head. During pre-training the head is an MLP with one hidden layer; for fine-tuning it is a single linear layer.
Fine-tuning swaps exactly one box: the pretrained head is thrown away and a fresh D x K layer for your K classes takes its place. Everything else starts from pretrained weights.

blocks.md: In code, the projection E is usually a convolution with kernel size = stride = patch size, for example `nn.Conv2d(3, 768, kernel_size=16, stride=16)` in Hugging Face's `ViTPatchEmbeddings`. Non-overlapping 16x16 windows times one shared weight is exactly a linear map applied to each flattened patch.

blocks.question: You feed a 384x384 image to a ViT-B/16 (patch size stays 16). How long is the sequence the encoder processes?
options: 197, because the model was built for 224x224 and the extra pixels are cropped
577: a 24x24 grid of patches plus the CLS token
576: one token per patch, since the CLS token is only used at 224
1153, because the patch count scales with the image side length times 3 channels
blocks.explain: 384 / 16 = 24 patches per side, so 576 patches, plus CLS: 577. The transformer itself accepts any sequence length (up to memory); what does not fit is the table of 197 position embeddings, which is the subject of lesson 3.

blocks.question: In Hugging Face's `ViTForImageClassification`, which vector does the classifier read?
options: The average of all 197 output vectors
The output at the last patch position, like a decoder LLM
The final hidden state at position 0, the CLS token
A concatenation of all 196 patch outputs
blocks.explain: The source takes `sequence_output[:, 0, :]` (position 0 is CLS) and passes it to `self.classifier`, a single `nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_labels)`. Averaging patch outputs is a valid alternative design (global average pooling), but it is not what this class does.

blocks.md: Every fine-tuning decision later in this course (which parameters to train, how much memory you need, what a resolution change touches) is easier once you know where the weights sit. ViT-Base, per Table 1 of the paper, has 12 layers, hidden size $D = 768$, MLP size 3072 and 12 attention heads, about 86M parameters. Let's recover that number from the architecture alone.

blocks.caption: Per block, with M = 3072 the MLP width. The number of heads does not appear: heads split the D columns, they do not add weights.

blocks.title: Parameters in one ViT-B/16 encoder block

scenes.caption: Attention side. Q, K and V are three D x D matrices with biases: 3 x (768 x 768 + 768) = 1,771,776. The output projection adds 590,592. Each LayerNorm has a scale and a shift: 2 x 768 = 1,536.
MLP side. fc1 maps 768 to 3072 (2,362,368 with bias) and fc2 maps back (2,360,064). The MLP holds 4,722,432 parameters, about two thirds of the block's 7,087,872.
Simplified view of where LoRA will act in lesson 5: it adds a small update next to the query and value matrices only, two of the 768 x 768 weights in this block.

blocks.prompt: Before the full count: what fraction of all ViT-B/16 parameters do you think sit in the patch projection, CLS token and position embeddings combined?
blocks.reveal: Under 1%. Embeddings total $590{,}592 + 768 + 151{,}296 = 742{,}656$, which is 0.87% of the 85,798,656 backbone parameters. The 12 encoder blocks hold 99.1%. This is why changing the image resolution (which only reshapes the position table) is cheap in parameters but, as lesson 3 shows, not free in compute.

blocks.title: Counting every ViT-B/16 parameter
blocks.code:
D, M, L, P = 768, 3072, 12, 16    # ViT-Base, Table 1
patch = (P*P*3)*D + D             # conv/linear E + bias
cls   = D
pos   = (224//P)**2 + 1           # 197 slots
pos   = pos * D
ln    = 2*D
attn  = 3*(D*D + D) + (D*D + D)   # Q,K,V + out proj
mlp   = (D*M + M) + (M*D + D)
block = 2*ln + attn + mlp
body  = patch + cls + pos + L*block + ln
head  = D*1000 + 1000             # ImageNet-1k head
total = body + head

scenes.caption: The four numbers from Table 1 of the ViT paper (layers 12, width 768, MLP 3072; the 12 heads split D and add no parameters) plus patch size 16.
Embedding side: E is 768 x 768 plus bias, one CLS vector, and 197 position vectors of size 768.
One encoder block, as in the bar chart: two LayerNorms, attention, MLP.
Twelve blocks dominate: 85,054,464 of the backbone's 85,798,656 parameters (99.1%). Position embeddings are only 0.18% of it.
With a 1000-class head the total is 86,567,656, the paper's "86M". For 101 food classes the head is 768 x 101 + 101 = 77,669 and the total is 85,876,325.

blocks.md: A ViT-B/16 backbone is 85.8M parameters, 99% of them in 12 identical blocks of 7.09M each, and two thirds of each block is MLP. The classification head is tiny: 77,669 parameters for 101 classes.

Library checkpoints may differ slightly from this count. Hugging Face's `ViTModel` can include an extra pooler layer (a D x D dense plus tanh); `ViTForImageClassification` builds the backbone without it and reads the raw CLS state. Always check with a parameter count on the actual model rather than trusting a model card.

blocks.question: You switch from 224x224 to 384x384 inputs on ViT-B/16. Which parameter tensor has to change shape?
options: Every Q, K and V matrix, because the sequence is longer
The patch projection E, because there are more patches
Only the position embedding table, from 197 x 768 to 577 x 768
None: the model handles any resolution without changes
blocks.explain: Attention and MLP weights act on each token's D-vector, so their shapes depend on D, not on sequence length. E acts on each 16x16x3 patch, unchanged. Only the learned table has one row per slot, so it must grow from 197 to 577 rows.

blocks.question: A colleague proposes ViT-B with 16 heads instead of 12 (D stays 768) to get more capacity. How does the parameter count of a block change?
options: It stays the same: each head gets 48 dims instead of 64
It grows by one third, since each head has its own Q, K, V
It doubles, because attention cost is quadratic
It shrinks, because the MLP gets smaller
blocks.explain: Multi-head attention splits the D = 768 output columns of Q, K and V among the heads. With 16 heads each head has 768 / 16 = 48 dims; the matrices are still 768 x 768. More heads changes how capacity is used, not how many weights exist.

lessons.title: A new head and a higher resolution

blocks.md:
Fine-tuning starts with surgery on the checkpoint. The ViT paper removes the whole pre-training head (two linear layers) and attaches a single **zero-initialized** D x K linear layer, where K is the number of target classes. The authors report this was a little more robust than re-initializing only the very last layer.

With all-zero weights and biases every class gets logit 0 at step one, so the first prediction is uniform over K classes. Libraries may initialize the new head differently (Hugging Face prints a warning that `classifier.weight` and `classifier.bias` are newly initialized). Either way, that layer has seen none of your data yet.

The second common change is resolution. Following earlier CNN work, the paper notes that it is often beneficial to fine-tune at a *higher* resolution than pre-training, and by default it fine-tunes at 384x384 after pre-training at 224. The patch size stays 16, so the grid grows from 14x14 to 24x24 and the sequence from 197 to 577 tokens.

The transformer accepts the longer sequence, but the 196 learned patch position embeddings were trained for a 14x14 layout. The paper's fix: **2D interpolation of the pre-trained position embeddings, according to their location in the original image**. Reshape the 196 vectors back to a 14x14 grid of 768 channels, resize the grid like an image to 24x24, and flatten again.

blocks.title: One row of one position-embedding channel, 14 to 24

scenes.caption: Toy: one channel of the position embeddings along one grid row, made smooth on purpose (sin values, rounded). A real ViT-B/16 table has 768 channels on a 14x14 grid; the operation is the same per channel.
At 384 the grid is 24 wide. New slot i sits at old coordinate (i + 0.5) x 14/24 - 0.5. Slot 5 lands at 2.71, between old slots 2 and 3, so its value comes from that neighborhood.
Bicubic interpolation (PyTorch's convention, weights from 4 neighbors) fills all 24 slots. The wave keeps its shape: largest error against the true sine at the new positions is 0.05.
Done in 2D for all 768 channels, this yields 576 patch embeddings. The CLS slot has no grid position, so libraries keep its embedding unchanged and concatenate it back in front: 577 rows.

blocks.prompt: Interpolation is just averaging neighbors. Why might the choice between bilinear and bicubic resizing matter for a pretrained transformer?
blocks.reveal: Because the network was trained on embeddings of a certain size. DeiT (Touvron et al.) observes that bilinear interpolation of a vector from its neighbors reduces its $\ell_2$ norm compared to those neighbors, that these low-norm vectors are not adapted to the pretrained transformer, and that accuracy drops significantly if used without fine-tuning. DeiT therefore uses **bicubic** interpolation, which approximately preserves the norm. Hugging Face's `interpolate_pos_encoding` always uses bicubic, and timm's `resample_abs_pos_embed` uses it by default.

blocks.title: Average vector length after resizing a 14x14 grid to 24x24

scenes.caption: Simplified stress test: 196 random 64-dim vectors (no spatial smoothness), mean length 7.93. Learned embeddings are much smoother, so real losses are smaller.
Bilinear output is a weighted average of 4 neighbors. Averaging vectors that point in different directions shortens them: mean length falls to 5.38 (68% of the original).
Bicubic uses 16 neighbors with some negative weights, which partly cancels the shrinkage: 6.83 (86%). This is the norm argument DeiT gives for preferring bicubic.

blocks.md: The longer sequence costs compute. Linear layers scale with token count, so 577 vs 197 tokens is about 2.9x more work per layer, while the attention score matrix grows with the square, about $(577/197)^2 \approx 8.6$x. Simplified: real step time also depends on kernels and memory traffic. Higher-resolution fine-tuning trades accuracy for a large jump in cost.

blocks.code:
from transformers import AutoModelForImageClassification
import timm

# Hugging Face: new 101-way head, interpolate pos-emb at forward time
model = AutoModelForImageClassification.from_pretrained(
    "google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k",
    num_labels=101, id2label=id2label, label2id=label2id)
out = model(pixel_values=x384, interpolate_pos_encoding=True)

# timm: new head and a 384 position table resampled at load time
m = timm.create_model("vit_base_patch16_224.augreg_in21k",
                      pretrained=True, num_classes=101, img_size=384)
blocks.caption: Two common ways to get a new head and a 384x384 model. x384 is a batch of 384x384 images, normalized like the checkpoint expects.

blocks.md: Preprocessing must match the checkpoint. `google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k` normalizes with mean 0.5 and std 0.5 per channel, while many timm ImageNet models use mean (0.485, 0.456, 0.406). Load the checkpoint's own settings (`AutoImageProcessor` in Transformers, `resolve_data_config` in timm) instead of copying numbers from another model.

blocks.question: Why does DeiT resize position embeddings with bicubic rather than bilinear interpolation?
options: Bicubic is faster on GPUs
Bilinear interpolation shrinks the vectors' norm, and short embeddings hurt the pretrained network
Bilinear cannot resize a 14x14 grid to 24x24 because 24 is not a multiple of 14
Bicubic interpolates the CLS embedding too, which bilinear cannot
blocks.explain: DeiT's stated reason is the norm: averaging neighbors shortens vectors, and those low-norm embeddings are out of distribution for the pretrained blocks. Both methods handle any target size, and the CLS embedding is not interpolated at all; it is kept as is.

blocks.question: After loading a 224 checkpoint, you fine-tune at 384 but forget `interpolate_pos_encoding=True` in Hugging Face. What happens?
options: Training silently runs at 224 because the processor crops
The model interpolates anyway, the flag only changes the method
It fails: the 197-row position table does not fit a 577-token sequence
Accuracy is identical, because position embeddings matter little
blocks.explain: Without the flag, the HF embedding layer checks the input size and raises a ValueError (input 384*384 does not match model 224*224); the 197-row table could not be added to 577 tokens anyway. Interpolation happens only when you ask for it.

lessons.title: The recipe: schedule, augmentation, per-layer learning rates

blocks.md:
The training loop is the one from the prerequisite course: forward pass, cross-entropy loss, backward pass, optimizer step. What changes for fine-tuning is the settings. The ViT paper fine-tunes with SGD with momentum 0.9, batch size 512, cosine learning-rate decay, no weight decay, gradient clipping at global norm 1, and a small learning-rate sweep (for example 0.001 to 0.03). Runs are short: 500 steps for Oxford-IIIT Pets and Flowers-102, 10,000 for CIFAR, 20,000 for ImageNet.

The Hugging Face image classification guide fine-tunes `google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k` on a 5,000-image slice of Food-101 with the Trainer, `learning_rate=5e-5`, a short warmup and 3 epochs. Both follow the same shape: a warmup, then a decaying rate.

blocks.caption: Linear warmup for w steps to the peak rate, then cosine decay to 0 at step T.

blocks.title: Linear warmup then cosine decay over 1000 steps

scenes.caption: Peak 5e-5 (the HF guide's learning rate), 100 warmup steps. The rate climbs linearly from 0 to 5e-5, so at step 50 it is 2.5e-5.
Cosine decay: halfway through the decay phase (step 550) the rate is exactly half the peak, 2.5e-5; at step 325 it is still 4.27e-5. It stays high longer than linear decay, then flattens near 0.

Why warm up at all: the new head starts with no knowledge of your classes, so early gradients are large and poorly aimed. A small rate for the first steps limits how far they push the pretrained blocks. Try w = 1.
Longer warmup, higher peak: a recipe closer to LoRA or linear probing, where few parameters train and larger rates are normal (the PEFT guide uses 5e-3 for LoRA, far off this chart).

blocks.md:
**Augmentation** fights overfitting when you have few images. The HF guide applies `RandomResizedCrop` and normalization during training. DeiT (Touvron et al., 2020) showed how far augmentation can go: it trains ViT-B on ImageNet-1k alone, without extra data, to 81.8% at 224 and 83.1% after fine-tuning at 384, and concludes that transformers require strong augmentation. Its recipe includes RandAugment, Mixup, CutMix, random erasing, repeated augmentation, stochastic depth and label smoothing 0.1 (dropout was excluded).

- **RandAugment** (Cubuk et al.) replaces a learned policy with two numbers: apply N operations chosen uniformly from a list of 14 (rotate, shear, contrast, solarize and so on), all at one global magnitude M. Larger N and M mean stronger regularization.
- **Mixup** (Zhang et al.) trains on blends of two examples and their labels:

blocks.caption: With one-hot labels: lambda = 0.7 on a cat image and a dog image gives a 70/30 pixel blend with target 0.7 cat, 0.3 dog.

blocks.md: Augmentation is a training-time tool. At evaluation use only the checkpoint's deterministic resize, center crop and normalization; random crops or Mixup at test time just add noise to your accuracy estimate.

**Layer-wise learning-rate decay** (LLRD) gives each depth its own rate. Lower layers learn generic features (edges, textures) that transfer well, so they should move less than the top layers and the new head. BEiT (Bao et al.) fine-tunes with this and lists decay 0.65 for ViT-Base and 0.75 for ViT-Large. In the [BEiT fine-tuning code](https://github.com/microsoft/unilm/blob/master/beit/run_class_finetuning.py), with L blocks, group i (0 = embeddings, 1 to L = blocks, L+1 = head) gets multiplier $d^{\,L+1-i}$. timm's training script exposes the same idea as `--layer-decay`.

blocks.title: Layer-wise LR decay: multiplier on the base learning rate

scenes.caption: Without layer decay every parameter group uses the base rate (multiplier 1).
Decay d = 0.75 (BEiT's value for ViT-Large): head 1, block 12 gets 0.75, block 8 0.237, block 1 0.032, embeddings 0.024.
Decay d = 0.65 (BEiT's value for ViT-Base): block 1 now learns at 0.0057 of the head's rate, about 176x slower, and the patch and position embeddings at 0.0037. Early, generic features barely move.

blocks.prompt: With BEiT's ViT-Base setting (d = 0.65, 12 blocks) and a base rate of 4e-3, what learning rate does the first encoder block get?
blocks.reveal: Block 1 is group $i = 1$, so its multiplier is $0.65^{12} \approx 0.00569$. Its rate is $4 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.00569 \approx 2.3 \times 10^{-5}$, while the head trains at the full $4 \times 10^{-3}$. One base rate, a 176x spread across depth.

blocks.question: A Mixup example blends image A (class 3) with image B (class 7) using lambda = 0.7. What is the training target?
options: Class 3 only, since lambda > 0.5
A vector with 0.7 at class 3 and 0.3 at class 7
A vector with 0.5 at class 3 and 0.5 at class 7
Class 7 only, since the second image is on top
blocks.explain: Mixup blends labels with the same lambda as the pixels: $\tilde{y} = 0.7\, y_3 + 0.3\, y_7$. The loss is cross-entropy against this soft target, which discourages overconfident predictions between classes.

blocks.question: You fine-tune with LLRD (d = 0.65) and see that the new head learns well but validation accuracy plateaus early and well below a full fine-tune with no decay. What is the most likely cause?
options: The decay is too strong for a dataset far from the pretraining data, so lower blocks can barely adapt
Warmup is too long, so the head never trains
Cosine decay is incompatible with LLRD
Position embeddings were not interpolated
blocks.explain: With d = 0.65 the bottom blocks get under 1% of the base rate. That is a good prior when pretrained features fit your task, but for a large domain gap (say, microscopy after natural images) the low layers need to move. Raise d toward 1 or raise the base rate. The other options do not match the symptom of a well-trained head with capped accuracy.

lessons.title: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train

blocks.md:
Three ways to adapt a pretrained ViT, from cheapest to most flexible:

- **Linear probe (LP)**: freeze the backbone, compute the CLS features once, train only a linear classifier on them. CLIP (Radford et al.) uses this as its standard evaluation of representation quality: scikit-learn logistic regression with L-BFGS on frozen image features, with the L2 strength swept on validation data.
- **Parameter-efficient fine-tuning** such as **LoRA**: freeze the backbone, add a small trainable update to some weight matrices.
- **Full fine-tuning (FT)**: train every parameter, starting from the checkpoint.

scenes.caption: Full fine-tuning trains all 85,876,325 parameters. The other two bars are there but under 1% of this height, which is the point.
Linear probe: freeze the backbone, train only the 768 x 101 + 101 = 77,669 head parameters (0.09% of the model).
LoRA r = 16 on query and value in all 12 blocks: 12 x 2 x 16 x (768 + 768) = 589,824 adapter parameters, plus the head: 667,493 (0.77% of 86,466,149). This matches the PEFT guide's printout.

blocks.md: LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) was introduced for large language models but applies to any linear layer, including ViT's attention projections. For a frozen weight $W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ it learns $\Delta W = BA$ with $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$ and a small rank $r$. A starts random Gaussian and B starts at zero, so training begins exactly at the pretrained model. The paper applies LoRA to the query and value projections in most experiments, and the Hugging Face PEFT image classification guide does the same for ViT (`target_modules=["query", "value"]`, with the new `classifier` fully trained via `modules_to_save`).

blocks.tex: h = W_0 x + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A x, \qquad \#\text{params} = r(d + k) \ll d k
blocks.caption: For d = k = 768 and r = 16: 24,576 trainable numbers instead of 589,824 per matrix.

scenes.caption: The pretrained query (or value) matrix W0 is frozen: no gradients, no optimizer state for its 589,824 weights.
A side path squeezes x to r = 16 numbers (A) and expands back (B). B starts at zero, so at step 0 the model is exactly the pretrained one.
Only A and B train: 16 x 768 + 768 x 16 = 24,576 parameters per matrix. After training, W = W0 + (alpha/r) BA can be merged into one matrix, so inference costs nothing extra.

blocks.md: Fewer trainable parameters means no gradients or Adam moments for the frozen weights, so memory drops and larger batches fit. The PEFT guide also uses a much larger learning rate for LoRA (5e-3) than typical full fine-tuning.

Is full fine-tuning always the accuracy winner? Kumar et al. (2022) tested this across 10 distribution shifts using strong pretrained features (MoCo-v2 ResNets and CLIP models, including a CLIP ViT-B/16 for ImageNet). Their finding: full fine-tuning **distorts** pretrained features. While a randomly initialized head is still wrong, its large gradients reshape the features of the training images, and features of out-of-distribution images change less, so the tuned head no longer fits them.

blocks.title: LP vs FT vs LP-FT, averages from Kumar et al. (2022)

scenes.caption: In-distribution (ID, average of 6 datasets): fine-tuning beats linear probing, 85.1% vs 82.9%. This is the well-known result.
Out-of-distribution (OOD, average of 10 shifts such as ImageNet-R and ImageNet-Sketch): the order flips. Linear probing 66.2%, fine-tuning 59.3%.
LP-FT, linear probe first and then fine-tune everything, is best on both: 85.7% ID and 68.9% OOD.

blocks.md: Their fix, **LP-FT**, is a two-step recipe: first train the head with the backbone frozen (a linear probe), then fine-tune everything starting from that head. Because the head is already good, gradients into the backbone are smaller; the paper measures feature changes 10 to 100 times smaller than plain fine-tuning. In their ImageNet runs each LP-FT stage got half the epochs of plain fine-tuning, so the compute was the same.

blocks.caption: Schematic: `train` is your usual loop. The learning rates echo the paper's ImageNet sweep ranges (larger for probing, smaller for fine-tuning); tune them for your data.

blocks.md: Decide by data and shift. Little data or a frozen-feature baseline needed: linear probe. Many tasks on one backbone or tight memory: LoRA (adapters are tiny and merge for free). Plenty of data from the deployment distribution: full fine-tune. Expect distribution shift at deployment: probe first, then fine-tune (LP-FT).

Kumar et al. note fine-tuning can still beat linear probing out of distribution when the pretrained features are weak or the shift is small (CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-10.1). LP-FT is a strong default, not a law.

blocks.question: A hospital fine-tunes an ImageNet-21k ViT on 3,000 X-rays from scanner A; it will be deployed on scanner B, which produces visibly different images. Which plan best matches the evidence in this lesson?
options: Full fine-tune with a randomly initialized head, since it has the highest in-distribution accuracy
Train only the position embeddings
LP-FT: fit the head on frozen features first, then fine-tune all layers
Skip training and use the ImageNet head directly
blocks.explain: Deployment shift is exactly where Kumar et al. found fine-tuning from a random head loses to probing, and where LP-FT won on 10 of 10 OOD datasets. The ImageNet head predicts ImageNet classes, and position embeddings alone cannot learn new classes.

blocks.question: You train LoRA (r = 16 on query and value) for ViT-B/16 and then merge the adapters with W = W0 + (alpha/r)BA. Compared with the original model, the merged model at inference has:
options: The same parameter count and the same latency
About 590K more parameters and a slightly slower forward pass
Half the parameters, since A and B replace W0
Lower accuracy, because merging rounds the update to low rank
blocks.explain: Merging adds BA into the existing matrices, so shapes are unchanged and so is the forward cost. The LoRA paper stresses this property: no additional inference latency compared with a fully fine-tuned model. The update was low rank during training too, so merging loses nothing.

blocks.question: Your linear probe on frozen ViT features gets 91% on your validation set; full fine-tuning gets 90%. What does this most likely tell you?
options: Fine-tuning code has a bug, because FT always wins in distribution
The pretrained features already separate your classes well; fine-tuning (maybe with too high a learning rate or too little data) is not adding much
Linear probing is overfitting, since it has fewer parameters
You should switch to a larger patch size
blocks.explain: Probing is a strong baseline whenever the features are good, which is why CLIP reports it. FT usually wins slightly in distribution, but not always: with little data or an aggressive learning rate it can distort useful features. Try a lower learning rate, LLRD or LP-FT before concluding anything.
